care: Paradise Lost tells the Bible's story of the Fall with a war in Heaven, a grim allegory of Sin and Death, and Adam and Eve's innocent life and marriage in Eden. The lesson summarizes these parts briefly and without detail. Young readers can begin with Books I, IV and XII, or a retelling.

young.html: John Milton was an English poet who went completely blind in his forties. He did not stop writing. He made up his poems in his head, sometimes in the night, and in the morning he spoke them aloud while a helper wrote them down. That is how he made Paradise Lost, one of the longest and grandest poems in English.

It retells the story from the beginning of the Bible. An angel named Satan rebels against God and is thrown out of Heaven. To get revenge, he travels to the new world God has made and finds the first people, Adam and Eve, in the beautiful Garden of Eden. He tricks Eve into eating fruit from the one tree God told them not to touch. Adam eats too, and they must leave the garden.
But the poem does not end in despair. An angel shows Adam that there is still hope for the future, and Adam and Eve walk out into the wide world together, hand in hand.

young.name: gb-pl-cosmos
young.cap: Milton's universe: Heaven, Chaos, Hell, and our world hanging on a golden chain. Follow the story.

young.html: Poet in the dark. Close your eyes (or wear a blindfold) and make up four lines about your favorite place. Say them to a grown-up, who writes them down. Then open your eyes and read them together. Was it harder or easier than writing? Imagine making a whole book this way, as Milton did.

full.html: John Milton (1608–1674) was a scholar-poet who spent the 1640s and 1650s writing prose for the Puritan and Parliamentary cause in England's civil wars, and served the government of the Commonwealth as Secretary for Foreign Tongues. He was totally blind by about 1652. When the monarchy returned in 1660 he was briefly arrested and lived afterward in retirement. Paradise Lost appeared in 1667 in ten books; the second edition of 1674 rearranged it into twelve.

Milton chose the highest subject he could imagine: the first disobedience of humankind, told in the form of the ancient epics of Homer and Virgil but in English, and with a Christian story. The poem is in blank verse, unrhymed lines of ten syllables, which Milton defended as the true English heroic verse.

full.text:
Of Man's first disobedience, and the fruit
Of that forbidden tree whose mortal taste
Brought death into the World, and all our woe,
With loss of Eden, till one greater Man
Restore us, and regain the blissful seat,
Sing, Heavenly Muse, …
full.author: John Milton
full.ed: 2nd edition, S. Simmons, London; Project Gutenberg text

full.html: A few lines later Milton states his purpose:

full.text:
That, to the height of this great argument,
I may assert Eternal Providence,
And justify the ways of God to men.
full.author: John Milton
full.ed: 2nd edition, S. Simmons, London; Project Gutenberg text

items: I–II. Satan and the rebel angels lie in Hell. They build a palace, Pandemonium, and hold a council. Satan sets out alone across Chaos to find the new world.
III. In Heaven, God foresees the Fall; the Son offers himself to redeem humankind. Satan, disguised, reaches the world.
IV. Eden. Satan sees Adam and Eve and envies their happiness. The guardian angels drive him away.
V–VIII. The angel Raphael visits Adam to warn him, and tells of Satan's rebellion, the war in Heaven and the creation of the world. Adam tells of his own creation and of meeting Eve.
IX. Satan, in the form of a serpent, persuades Eve to eat the forbidden fruit. Adam, unwilling to lose her, eats too.
X. Judgment. Adam and Eve quarrel, then reconcile and repent.
XI–XII. The angel Michael shows Adam the future, up to the promise of redemption. Adam and Eve leave Eden together.

full.name: gb-pl-cosmos
full.cap: Where each part of the poem takes place. Milton hangs the newly created world from Heaven by a golden chain, above Chaos.

full.html: Satan is the first great speaker in the poem, and many readers find him the most vivid character. In Book I, having lost Heaven, he claims his own mind will be his kingdom:

full.text:
The mind is its own place, and in itself
Can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven.
full.author: John Milton
full.ed: 2nd edition, S. Simmons, London; Project Gutenberg text

full.html: The poem shows this boast to be false. Satan carries his Hell within him wherever he goes, and as the poem goes on he shrinks, from a fallen archangel to a toad, a serpent, and at last a hissing snake among snakes.

Freedom is at the center of Milton's argument. In Book III God says he made angels and humans free to stand or fall, because obedience that is not freely chosen would be worth nothing. This is Milton's answer to why God allowed the Fall.

Thinking Milton simply copied Genesis. The Bible's account takes a few pages; Milton adds the war in Heaven, the council of devils, long conversations, and the inner lives of Adam and Eve, drawn from tradition and his own imagination.

deep.html: Readers have argued for three centuries about Satan. The poet William Blake wrote that Milton was “of the Devil's party without knowing it,” meaning that Milton's imagination came alive in Satan's rebellion. Many other critics answer that the poem deliberately makes Satan attractive at first, so that readers feel the pull of his arguments and then see through them. The poem itself presents Satan's cause as false.

Milton was a deeply religious Protestant who held independent views. A Latin treatise on Christian doctrine, found in 1823, showed that he differed from most churches of his day on some points of theology. Scholars still discuss how far those views appear in the poem. Samuel Johnson, who admired the poem greatly, said that “none ever wished it longer than it is,” which is both praise and a joke.

Later poets wrote in Milton's shadow: Wordsworth called on him in a sonnet, and the Romantics read Satan as a rebel hero. In the 19th century, Mary Shelley's creature in Frankenstein reads Paradise Lost and compares himself to both Adam and Satan.

items: Is obedience worth anything if you had no choice?
Can a story make a wrong side sound convincing, and what should a reader do about that?
Is it true that “the mind is its own place”? In what ways?

questions: Milton wrote his greatest poem after going blind. What helps a person keep going after a big loss?
Why do you think the poem begins with Satan instead of with Adam and Eve?
Have you ever been persuaded by someone who turned out to be wrong? How did you see through it?
God in the poem says freely chosen love is the only kind worth having. Do you agree?
The poem ends with Adam and Eve walking out together. Is that a sad ending, a hopeful one, or both?
